---
title: "Bayes' rule"
---

Suppose a pronunciation feature is strongly associated with a small dialect group. Hearing the feature may provide evidence about a speaker's dialect, but the strength of that evidence cannot be read directly from the rate of the feature within the group. We need to reverse the direction of a conditional probability.

The [preceding page](probability-factorization.qmd) gave two applications of the product rule to the same intersection:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

Since the left sides are identical, the right sides are equal:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
=\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

If $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, divide both sides by $\mathbb{P}(C)$:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B)}
       {\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

This identity is [**Bayes' rule**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). It is not a new probability axiom. It follows from applying the product rule to one joint event in two orders.

## Check the derivation with pronouns

Let $A$ again be the accusative event and $P$ the plural event. We want $\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)$. Bayes' rule gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)}
       {\mathbb{P}(P)}.
$$

The values from the joint table are

$$
\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)=\frac{.40}{.70},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(A)=.70,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(P)=.50.
$$

Substituting them gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
&=\frac{(.40/.70)\times.70}{.50}\\
&=\frac{.40}{.50}\\
&=.80.
\end{aligned}
$$

The result matches the direct conditional probability calculation. Bayes' rule reaches the same quantity from the reversed conditional and the two event probabilities.

## Work through a dialect feature

Now let $D$ be membership in a dialect group and $F$ be use of a pronunciation feature. Imagine a represented population of 1,000 tokens with these counts.

| | feature $F$ | no feature $F^c$ | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| dialect group $D$ | 90 | 10 | 100 |
| other group $D^c$ | 180 | 720 | 900 |
| total | 270 | 730 | 1,000 |

Within the dialect group, the feature is very common:

$$
\mathbb{P}(F\mid D)=\frac{90}{100}=.90.
$$

We want the reversed probability, the probability of group membership given the feature:

$$
\mathbb{P}(D\mid F).
$$

The other required values are

$$
\mathbb{P}(D)=\frac{100}{1000}=.10
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(F)=\frac{270}{1000}=.27.
$$

Bayes' rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(D\mid F)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(F\mid D)\mathbb{P}(D)}
        {\mathbb{P}(F)}\\
&=\frac{.90\times.10}{.27}\\
&=\frac{1}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The feature occurs in ninety percent of dialect group tokens, but only one third of all feature tokens come from that group. The group is small, and the feature also occurs outside it. Bayes' rule incorporates both facts.

```{r}
#| eval: false
p_feature_given_dialect <- .90
p_dialect <- .10
p_feature <- .27

p_dialect_given_feature <-
  p_feature_given_dialect * p_dialect / p_feature

p_dialect_given_feature
```

The result is approximately `.333`.

## Read the terms as evidence and prevalence

In the dialect calculation, $\mathbb{P}(F\mid D)$ states how compatible the feature is with the group. The probability $\mathbb{P}(D)$ states how prevalent the group is in the represented population. The denominator $\mathbb{P}(F)$ states how common the feature is overall.

All three quantities are tied to an observation process. A sample balanced to contain equal numbers of speakers from two groups does not directly provide the population value of $\mathbb{P}(D)$. Using the sample proportion would answer a question about the balanced sample unless the design is adjusted to represent the target population.

## A common failure: transposing conditional probabilities

The [error of transposing a conditional probability](conditional-probability.qmd#a-common-failure-transposing-conditional-probabilities) occurs when $\mathbb{P}(F\mid D)$ is treated as if it were $\mathbb{P}(D\mid F)$. The transposition removes the prevalence term $\mathbb{P}(D)$ and ignores how often $F$ occurs outside $D$.

A highly characteristic feature may still identify a small share of observed feature tokens when the relevant group is rare. The count table provides a useful check because the reversed conditional can be read directly as $90/270$, not $90/100$.

## Check your understanding

1. Derive Bayes' rule by equating the two product rule expressions for $B\cap C$.
2. In the dialect table, compute $\mathbb{P}(F\mid D^c)$ and $\mathbb{P}(D^c\mid F)$.
3. Explain in words why $.90$ and $1/3$ answer different questions.
4. If the dialect group made up half of the represented population while the two within group feature rates stayed fixed, would $\mathbb{P}(D\mid F)$ increase or decrease? Explain without introducing a new formula.

Bayes' rule reverses a conditional probability while retaining the event prevalences. The [next page](independence.qmd) asks when conditioning does not change a probability at all.
